explainer.label: Computational physics
explainer.title: A Star Trek hologram, with today's lasers
explainer.lede: We asked one question: can you build a true 3D image that floats in open air, the kind of hologram you see in Star Trek, from parts you can order today? We simulated the physics end to end, and the answer is yes.
steps: Two invisible laser beams, each too weak to do anything on its own, meet at one point in the air.
Where they meet, the air turns into a tiny spark of light: one pixel with a real address in space.
Move about 10,000 of those points 60 times a second and you see a floating image you can walk around and pass your hand through.
facts: Prototype priced from real vendor catalogues
Photons per point reach the eye, where about 100 are enough to see it
Simulations across nine areas of physics, from quantum chemistry to plasma
Published references, each verified by its DOI
explainer.honest: What it is, and isn't: a computational study, not a working device. No laser was switched on. Every number comes from open-source physics simulators run by an AI agent, and the image would be line art (outlines, text, shapes), not a solid picture.
explainer.figure: Computed, not photographed: cross the two beams at a wider angle and the glow shrinks from a streak (left) to a single point (right).
